subject: geography

moments.title: Köppen's first classification
moments.body: Köppen publishes a global classification based on temperature and rainfall thresholds linked to vegetation zones. He revises it repeatedly through 1918 and into the 1930s with his son-in-law Rudolf Geiger.
moments.takeaway: Climate classification before Köppen was largely based on latitude bands. He used measurable climatic variables tied to ecological outcomes.

moments.title: Final Köppen-Geiger classification
moments.body: The mature classification uses five main groups (A tropical, B arid, C temperate, D continental, E polar) with second and third letters for precipitation and temperature subtypes. Cfb (UK), Csa (Mediterranean), BSh (semi-arid hot) and so on.
moments.takeaway: Maps of Köppen zones still appear in nearly every introductory geography text. They show climate types as discrete regions — an approximation that hides gradients.

now.title: Climates on the move
now.body: Recent updates (Beck et al., 2018, 2023) show Köppen-Geiger zones shifting under climate change. By 2100, around 12-30% of land area is projected to change classification under RCP8.5. Mediterranean climates are spreading polewards. Some classifications no longer match the vegetation they originally identified.
now.open_questions: Is a 19th-century vegetation-tied classification still the right tool? Bioclimatic models (e.g. Holdridge life zones, the Whittaker biome diagram) compete for ecological work.

reflection: Köppen made climate visible as a system of types. The system's age — designed for a stable climate — is now itself a problem. The categories are moving on a map drawn under different assumptions.
